content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued recommendations regarding the use of home-based records (HBRs) for maternal, newborn, and child health. These records are designed to improve health outcomes by providing parents and caregivers with accessible, paper-based documentation of health information. Below are detailed descriptions of studies and interventions related to HBRs, their outcomes, and their specific focus areas: 1. Magwood et al. (2018): Intervention: Parents were provided with a child health record to enhance their knowledge of child health and illness. Outcomes: Improved communication between caregivers and healthcare providers, as well as increased utilization of healthcare services. Type of HBR: Paper-based, multi-focus, without a health education component. 2. Dagvadorj et al. (2017): Study Design: Cluster randomized controlled trial (cRCT) conducted in Mongolia. Intervention: Pregnant women received the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) handbook, which included information on pregnancy, delivery, postpartum health, child growth, immunization, and dental health. Outcomes: Reduced risk of developmental delays in children. Type of HBR: Paper-based, multi-focus, with a health education component. 3. Elbourne et al.: Intervention: Women retained their obstetric case notes throughout pregnancy and up to 10 days postpartum. Comparison: Women who only held a small, abbreviated card. Outcomes: Increased feelings of control and satisfaction during pregnancy. Type of HBR: Paper-based, single-focus, without a health education component. 4. Lakhani et al.: Intervention: Parents were given a home-based child health booklet. Outcomes: Improved caregiver knowledge of child health, better communication between caregivers and healthcare providers, and enhanced continuity of care. Type of HBR: Paper-based, multi-focus, without a health education component. 5. Lovell et al.: Intervention: Women were provided with their maternity case notes to keep until delivery. Outcomes: Increased antenatal care (ANC) visits, reduced smoking and alcohol consumption, and improved maternal and newborn health outcomes, including exclusive breastfeeding. Type of HBR: Paper-based, single-focus, without a health education component. 6. Moore et al.: Intervention: A supplementary child health record was provided for children with disabilities, in addition to the standard child health record. Comparison: No supplementary record provided. Outcomes: Improved usability, perceived value of healthcare, and communication between families and healthcare providers. Type of HBR: Paper-based, single-focus, without a health education component. 7. Mori et al.: Intervention: Women received the MCH handbook at the start of the study. Outcomes: Increased ANC visits, improved maternal physical and mental health, and better neonatal health outcomes. Type of HBR: Paper-based, multi-focus, with a health education component. 8. Osaki et al. (2018): Study Design: cRCT conducted in Indonesia. Intervention: Pregnant women received the MCH handbook, along with competency-based training for healthcare workers and monthly monitoring meetings. Comparison: No MCH handbook provided. Outcomes: Improved maternal and newborn health outcomes, including ANC visits, maternal immunization, exclusive breastfeeding, and child health knowledge. Type of HBR: Paper-based, multi-focus, with a health education component. 9. Stille et al. (2001): Study Design: Controlled trial in the USA. Intervention: Infants received a graphic immunization card with spaces for stickers and vaccination schedule information. Outcomes: Improved immunization status, including vaccination initiation and series completion. Type of HBR: Paper-based, single-focus, with a health education component. 10. Usman et al. (2009, 2011): Study Design: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in urban and rural Pakistan. Intervention: Mothers were provided with redesigned immunization cards and/or brief education sessions emphasizing the importance of completing the immunization schedule. Outcomes: Improved immunization status, including vaccination initiation and series completion. Type of HBR: Paper-based, single-focus, with a health education component. 11. Yanagisawa et al.: Intervention: Cambodian mothers received an MCH handbook modeled after Japanese and Indonesian versions. Comparison: Mothers received standard Cambodian child health and maternal health records. Outcomes: Increased ANC visits, skilled birth attendance, maternal knowledge of danger signs, exclusive breastfeeding, and child immunization rates. Type of HBR: Paper-based, multi-focus, with a health education component. These studies collectively highlight the potential of home-based records to improve maternal, newborn, and child health outcomes through better communication, increased health service utilization, and enhanced caregiver knowledge. The effectiveness of these interventions often depends on the inclusion of health education components and the design of the records themselves.
